title: 1.1.21 Does It Fit?
description: Four multiple-choice questions on prescriptive process models and where they break. Checked instantly.

questions.question: What does a prescriptive process model advocate?
options: Writing the code first and planning afterwards
An orderly, prescribed sequence of activities
Letting each developer choose their own order of work
questions.explanation: "Prescriptive" means it tells you what to do — an orderly, prescribed sequence. Nothing fancier.

questions.question: Which list gives examples of prescriptive process models?
questions.explanation: Waterfall, prototyping, spiral and RUP are named examples. The idea they share is the orderly sequence.

questions.question: Zara runs a startup, and her product requirements change every week as she talks to new customers. Does a prescriptive process model fit her project?
options: Yes — an orderly sequence is what will stop the requirements changing
Yes — startups are small, and prescriptive models suit small teams
No — prescriptive models only work for projects written in one language
No — prescriptive models are rigid, and hers is exactly the case they handle worst: requirements that keep changing
questions.explanation: Rigidity is the problem. A plan made once cannot bend to requirements that move every week.

questions.question: What does the rigid-recipe analogy capture about prescriptive models?
options: A recipe is easier to follow than code, so software should read like one
Anyone can follow a recipe, so anyone can run a software project
A strict recipe works start to finish, but fails when the situation changes mid-way
Recipes list ingredients first, and so should software plans
questions.explanation: Follow the recipe and it works — until something changes and the recipe has no room to bend. That is the failure mode.
